title: Remember, remember
hook: raam simar raam simar ihai tero kaaj hai: remember, this is your real work (Jaijavanti M9, ang 1352)

segments.voice: Yesterday, baas: the Lord lives within, like scent in a flower. If the One is that close, what do you do about it? Today's hymn gives a job.

A to-do list on a Monday morning. Reply to the landlord. Book the dentist. Finish the report. Buy milk. Call Mom back. Return the package. It's long, and everything on it feels urgent. Now imagine someone gently taking the pen and writing one more line at the very top, above all of it, underlined twice. Not instead of the list. Above it. Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymn in Raag Jaijavanti does exactly that. It opens with a word said twice, and then says what your real work is.
screen: `A MONDAY TO-DO LIST.` → `ONE LINE WRITTEN AT THE TOP.` → `A WORD SAID TWICE.`

segments.voice: The hymn opens raam simar, raam simar, ihai tero kaaj hai. Remember the Lord, remember the Lord: this is your work. Simar is the root of simran: remembering, keeping the Lord in mind, often by repeating the Name. Raam, in Gurbani, is the all-pervading One. And kaaj is work, the job you came to do. Why say it twice? Think of how you call someone who's drifting off: hey, hey. The doubling is a hand on the shoulder. Then, in paraphrase: leave the company of maya, and take shelter with the Lord. Know the world's pleasures to be false; all this show is passing. Know wealth as a dream; why be proud of it? The kingdom of the whole earth is like a wall of sand. And near the end, Nanak says the body will perish, as time slips away moment by moment. Here's the surprise. The hymn doesn't call remembering a hobby, or a reward for when the work is done. It calls it the work. Sikhs hear the same thought in a hymn of Guru Arjan's in the evening prayer: no other task will help you; join the holy company and meditate on the Name alone. So the list doesn't vanish. You still buy the milk and call your mother. But the line at the top changes the rest, because the other jobs no longer carry your whole worth. That's simran: the work under all the work.
screen: `RAAM SIMAR, RAAM SIMAR.` · `KAAJ: THE JOB YOU CAME TO DO.` · `WEALTH AS A DREAM, A WALL OF SAND.` · `THE WORK UNDER ALL THE WORK.` · then, large: `THIS IS YOUR WORK.`

segments.voice: Before the list, the phone or the inbox, sit and breathe slowly. If you pray, repeat Waheguru quietly, once on each breath, the way Sikhs practice simran; if you don't, come back again and again to the plain fact that you're here and alive. When the list starts calling, let it wait.
Remember. Raam simar, raam simar: Guru Tegh Bahadur says twice that remembering the Lord is your real work, the job under every other job.
Your line: this is your work. The list still gets done; it just isn't at the top. Day five hundred eighty-five, done.

howItsDone: Many Sikhs begin the day with simran, repeating Waheguru, before Nitnem and the day's work; Guru Tegh Bahadur's Jaijavanti shabad 'raam simar raam simar' is sung in kirtan as a call to that practice.

fork.setup: your to-do list is long and urgent. what does the Jaijavanti hymn say is your real work?
fork.reveal: raam simar, raam simar, ihai tero kaaj hai: remember the Lord, remember: this is your work.

original.note: Gurmukhi: simran, remembering, from the same root as the hymn's simar.

trapdoor: what you thought: remembering is something to do once the real work is finished.
what it means: the hymn says remembering is the real work, and everything else sits under it.
what a scholar hears: kaaj, purpose or task, echoes Guru Arjan's line in the evening prayer that no other task will help you; the ninth Guru restates the fifth Guru's teaching in his own plain words.

chat.says: When would I even have time to remember God? My to-do list is endless.
options: The hymn says remembering isn't extra; it's your real work, the line above the list.
The hymn says remember God once the list is finished, as a reward at the end.
The hymn says only a few holy people have that job; others just do their chores.
chat.meaning: Raam simar, raam simar, ihai tero kaaj hai: remembering is your kaaj, the work under all the work, not a reward for later.

simran.meaning: remembering the Lord, often by repeating the Name
